title: Member Functions
relevance: Interviewers probe member-function categories, definition with ::, object passing/returning, and const correctness as core C++ class design fluency.

phases.goal: Establish the conventional categories of member functions and where they may be defined.

must_hit.point: Member functions are conventionally grouped into four categories by role: Manager, Accessor (getter), Mutator (setter), and Utility (facilitator)—conventions, not distinct language features.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the four roles and notes they are conventions for managing object state, not separate language constructs.

must_hit.point: A member function may be defined inside the class body, or declared inside and defined outside using the scope resolution operator (::).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both placement options and mentions :: for the out-of-class definition.

must_hit.point: Static member functions operate on the class as a whole rather than a specific object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts static members with ordinary instance member functions.

probes: What are the main categories of member functions, and how do you define a member function outside its class?

hints.1: Think about how functions relate to object state: create/destroy, read, write, or compute.
hints.2: List Manager, Accessor, Mutator, Utility; then mention declaration in the class and definition with ClassName::.
hints.3: Four conventional roles; out-of-class definition uses the scope resolution operator so the compiler knows which class owns the function.

phases.goal: Explain inline rules, two-pass class parsing, const member functions, mutable, and ref-qualifiers.

must_hit.point: A function defined inside the class body is implicitly inline; defining outside the class but still wanting inline requires the explicit inline keyword.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes implicit inline for in-class definitions from the need for explicit inline when defined outside (e.g. in a header).

must_hit.point: Inside a class, definition order does not matter: the compiler parses declarations in a first pass and function bodies in a second pass, so a function near the top can call one declared near the bottom.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions two-pass parsing and that call order among members is independent of textual order.

must_hit.point: A const member function is declared by placing const after the parameter list; it must not modify the object's state, and only const member functions may be called on a const object (including via const reference).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows trailing const, no data-member mutation, and that non-const methods cannot be invoked on const instances.

must_hit.point: mutable on a data member exempts it from const enforcement so a const member function can change cache or mutex state while preserving logical constness.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives caching or thread-safety examples and contrasts logical vs bitwise constness.

must_hit.point: C++11 ref-qualified member functions append & or && to restrict calls to lvalues (persistent objects) or rvalues (temporaries).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains process() & vs process() && and when each overload is selected.

probes: What does it mean for a member function to be const, and what does mutable change about that guarantee?

hints.1: Look at where const appears on a member function and what the compiler allows inside its body.
hints.2: Trailing const means this is treated as const; mutable members can still be written for caches or mutexes.
hints.3: Only const methods on const objects; mutable enables logical constness when bitwise state changes without changing observable value.

phases.goal: Compare definition placement and how objects are passed or returned from member functions.

must_hit.point: Short functions (e.g. getters/setters) are often defined inside the class; longer or more complex functions are best declared in the class (header) and defined outside (typically in a .cpp) with ClassName::.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties in-class definition to convenience/short bodies and out-of-class to longer logic and header/.cpp split.

must_hit.point: Passing class-type objects by value copies the whole object via the copy constructor and is generally inefficient; prefer reference (&) or const reference (const &) when the argument should not be modified.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects default by-value for large objects and names const & as the usual read-only parameter form.

must_hit.point: Return by value when creating a new object (compilers may apply RVO); return by reference when returning an existing object such as *this for chaining—never a local.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates new-object returns from *this chaining and flags dangling references to locals.

probes: When would you define a member function inside the class versus outside, and how should you pass and return objects?

hints.1: Consider function length and whether you need to avoid copying large objects.
hints.2: Inside for short/inline-friendly code; outside with :: for complex logic; prefer const & parameters; value vs reference returns depend on new vs existing objects.
hints.3: In-class implies inline; out-of-class needs :: (and inline if kept in a header); almost always pass objects by const &; return value for new objects (RVO), reference for *this chaining.

phases.goal: Apply const correctness and safe return practices in realistic class APIs.

must_hit.point: Const correctness means marking member functions const when they do not modify state and passing objects as const Type& when modification is not intended; omitting const on an accessor blocks reads through const instances.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines the practice and explains the failure mode if getters lack const.

must_hit.point: Never return a reference to a local variable created inside the function; the local is destroyed at return, leaving a dangling reference—return by value when generating new objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the dangling-reference trap and the by-value fix for newly created objects.

must_hit.point: Ref-qualified overloads are an advanced tool used mainly to optimise return types or prevent dangerous operations on temporary objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a purpose for &/&& member overloads beyond basic const.

probes: What is const correctness, and why is returning a reference to a local from a member function unsafe?

hints.1: Think about const objects and what methods they are allowed to call.
hints.2: Mark non-mutating methods const and use const & parameters; locals die at function exit so references to them dangle.
hints.3: Without const on accessors, const instances cannot be read; always return by value for new objects, not a reference to a local.

tradeoffs.topic: Define inside class vs declare inside / define outside with ::
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Inside is convenient for short functions and is implicitly inline; longer or more complex functions should be declared in the class (often a header) and defined outside with ClassName:: (typically in a .cpp); if defined outside but still in a header and you want inline, mark inline explicitly.

tradeoffs.topic: Pass by value vs by reference / const reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: By value copies the whole object via the copy constructor and is generally inefficient for class types; almost always pass by & to avoid the copy, or const & when the function must not modify the argument.

tradeoffs.topic: Return by value vs by reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Return by value when creating a new object (RVO may eliminate the copy); return by reference when handing back an existing object such as *this for chaining; never return a reference to a local.
A const member function must not change observable state; mutable exempts specific members (e.g. caches, mutexes) so bitwise state may change while logical constness is preserved.

gotchas.trap: Returning a reference to a local variable created inside the function
gotchas.correction: The local is destroyed when the function ends, leaving a dangling reference; return by value when generating new objects.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting to mark an accessor as const
gotchas.correction: Users cannot call non-const methods on const instances (including via const reference), so unmarked getters block reading from const objects—const correctness requires const on non-mutating members and const Type& when modification is not intended.

gotchas.trap: Calling a non-const member function on a const object or const reference
gotchas.correction: The compiler treats the object as read-only, so only const member functions are allowed (e.g. getBalance() ok, deposit() error).

gotchas.trap: Assuming an out-of-class definition in a header is inline like an in-class definition
gotchas.correction: Only in-class definitions are implicitly inline; outside the class you must write the inline keyword explicitly if you want inline.
